blocks.text: KING OF ASSYRIA · TWO KINGDOMS
Esarhaddon. Sennacherib's son, who reigned after him; settlers he brought into the land dated their worship from his days.
REIGNEDi
Not given c. 680–669 BC (dates vary)

Nineveh

WHAT SCRIPTURE SAYS
What Scripture says of him
"And Esar-haddon his son reigned in his stead." 2 Kings 19:37 Isaiah 37:38
The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin told Zerubbabel: "we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esar-haddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither." Ezra 4:1–2
DEALINGS
Dealings with God's people
The settlers said they had sacrificed to Israel's God "since the days of Esar-haddon"; Zerubbabel and Jeshua refused their help with the temple. Ezra 4:2–3
From the textChronicles says "the captains of the host of the king of Assyria" took Manasseh to Babylon, but does not name the king; see the question below. 2 Chronicles 33:11

From the textThree passages speak of foreigners settled in Samaria: 2 Kings 17:24 ("the king of Assyria", unnamed), Ezra 4:2 (Esar-haddon) and Ezra 4:10 ("the great and noble Asnappar"). 2 Kings 17:24 Ezra 4:2 Ezra 4:10
EVENTS
Wars, works and turning points
UNDATED IN SCRIPTURE
DATES DIFFER
When was it?
LUCKENBILL (1927)
SCRIPTURE'S NUMBERS
No years given
Scripture gives no years for him (2 Kgs 19:37; Ezra 4:2).
ROGERS (1912)
THE BABYLONIAN CHRONICLE
No years given[73]
After Sennacherib's murder on the twentieth of Tebet, the revolt lasted until the second of Adar; Esarhaddon took the throne on the eighteenth of Adar.
Chronicles names none
2 Chronicles 33:11
"The captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon." 2 Chronicles 33:11
Esarhaddon
John Gill (1748–63); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); the Pulpit Commentary
Gill and Jamieson–Fausset–Brown name Esar-haddon; the Pulpit Commentary prefers Esarhaddon and thinks his son Assur-banipal less likely. 2 Chronicles 33:11 [55][65][45]
Asshur-bani-pal, his son
W. E. Barnes (1899); Ellicott's commentary (about 1880), tentatively

Barnes points to a great revolt against Asshur-bani-pal in which Western Asia, "and perhaps Manasseh", was involved; Ellicott's commentary says Esarhaddon's generals, "or rather, perhaps, of Assurbanipal". 2 Chronicles 33:11 [99][7]
The records are silent
the lists of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal
Both kings list Manasseh among their vassals; neither mentions a captivity.[37][38]

Every passage

PASSAGES · 4

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture records no campaign of Esarhaddon against Israel or Judah.
Scripture gives no length for his reign and does not say how he died.
Ezra 4:2 does not say where the settlers came from.
